In the beautiful stretch of country back of Greenwich, Conn., a mighty tribe of Indians are soon to meet, smoke the pipe of peace, and discuss the beloved forests. The braves will show their prowess with tomahawk and knife and vie with each other in mighty deeds of the hunt and in athletic sport. The smoke will rise from a hundred wigrams in the forest, and the twang of the bow will be heard and painted and be-feathered forms will slip through the gloaming. And by these signs the athletes will know that the gest encampment of Woodcraft Indians is on at Wyndygoul.

They are not real Indians, but healthy, happy American boys gather- ed together by Ernest Thompson Seton, the writer. Mr. Seton founded the tribe and established the encampment some five or six years ago. His object is to allow boys to live close to nature, not by mere living in the open, but by adopting the free life of the American Indian.

The boys responded with enthusiasm and within a very short time there were hundreds "hitting the trail" back into the past. They adopted the war whoop with the Indian dress. The tribe prospered until now, it is said there are 2,000 boys who hail Mr. Seton as Black Wolf, the Great Chief. The ages of the Indians range from ten to twenty years.

Mr. Seton's country place with excess acres of almost virgin land, and its magnificent lake is a splendid gathering place for the Woodcraft tribe. They come from New York, New Jersey, "up New England way" and even from the west, bringing with them there wigmans, hows and arrows, and Indian dress.

Most impressive is the service of adoption through which each new brave must enter the counsels of the tribe and then after adoption each one must earn his name. For example, Chief Split-the-Wind, a lively laid of 15 years, won his name because of his ability as a manner, "Steady-in-Arm," because he could shoot the mark; "Eagle Eye" can usually be depended upon to spy the game first, while "Much Fish" stands first in the winners of the surgeon game. This game like the other games of the tribe is interesting. Out in the center of the lake a big wooden block, roughly shaped like a fish, is set drift. At the same time fishing parties put out in canoes from both sides of the lake. The fisherman are armed with spears and the object is to spear the fish and bring it ashore. The other party tries to get the fish away and the side landing the fish on the bank wins the game.

The hunt is a test of skill. A stuffed deer is hidden on the depth of the wood. A lad wearing shoes to which are fastened iron plates leaving a mark as though a deep had really passed makes the trail. This done the hunting parties start out to follow the trail. They follow with heads down and eyes ever on the alert. The one who first spies the game makes so many points while more go to the fortunate shot who plants an arrow in a vital spot.

The enthusiastic youngsters learn to blaze a trail, read the language of the forest, carry in the wounded(?), build the camp fire and do a hundred other things once done by the Indians who roamed through Connect- out. Camp life includes athletic sports, diving swimming contests and other games that will appeal to every led whether he be American or Indian.

At night when darkness settles down on forest and lake and trail, the camp fires are lit, and great powwows are held. Black Wolf tells wonderful stories of beast and bird and many a Woodcraft Indian pulls his blanket over his head, afraid, no, anxious as to what lies in the darkness beyond the camp life.

BRIG.-GEN. SCRIVEN VIRIS INMACAN FROM. STUDIES SITUATION FOR AMERICAN GOVERNMENT.

Brigadier-General Georgi P. Scriven who is now on the front where the Italian forces are holding back the Austro-Tuuton armies, studying the situation for the American government. He has already inspected the line along the Upper Plave and is going to go along the northern fighting line.

Gen. Scriven went into the first line trenches along the Piave while the litions were subjecting them to a heavy artillery and rifle fire. The Italicians were replying over the place where the general end of his escorts were making it in inspection. He expressed himself afterwards as impressed very favorably with all that he saw, especially with the fine appearance of four batteries of artillery hesening along the roads up to the front line.
